title: OpenAPI 3.1 and API Contracts: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on OpenAPI 3.1 document structure, paths, schemas and components, design-first versus code-first, client generation, contract testing and keeping docs in sync.

chapters.title: OpenAPI 3.1 Mental Model and Document Structure
points: OpenAPI is a language-neutral, machine-readable contract (YAML or JSON) describing an HTTP API; Swagger UI, codegen, mocks and linters all read the same file
Top-level fields: openapi (version string, e.g. 3.1.0), info (title and version required), servers, paths, components, security, tags
info.version is the API's own version, not the OpenAPI spec version; the two are unrelated
3.1 aligns schemas with JSON Schema 2020-12 and adds a top-level webhooks map for provider-initiated calls; a document needs at least one of paths, components or webhooks
Interview Point: What is the difference between OpenAPI and Swagger? What are the required top-level fields? What did 3.1 change versus 3.0?

chapters.title: Paths, Operations and Parameters
points: A path item (/users/{id}) holds one operation per HTTP method (get, post, put, patch, delete); each operation has a unique operationId, which codegen uses as the method name
Parameters have in: path | query | header | cookie; path parameters must set required: true and match the {name} in the URL template
requestBody holds content keyed by media type (application/json) with a schema; responses are keyed by status code, plus an optional default for errors

In 3.1 an operation's responses field is optional, but when present it must list at least one status code (3.0 required it); document the error shapes (400, 401, 404, 422) as well as the 200/201 success case
Interview Point: Where can parameters be located? Why does operationId matter for client generation? How do you describe a request body and multiple responses?

chapters.title: Schemas, Components and $ref Reuse
points: components holds reusable schemas, parameters, responses, requestBodies, securitySchemes and examples; reference them with $ref: '#/components/schemas/User'
3.1 nullable is gone: write type: ['string','null'] instead of 3.0's nullable: true
3.1 allows $ref siblings (description, summary) and uses examples (array) instead of the old single example keyword; exclusiveMinimum and exclusiveMaximum are now numbers, not booleans
Compose with allOf (merge/extend), oneOf (exactly one match) and anyOf; add discriminator with propertyName so tools can pick the subtype for polymorphic payloads
Interview Point: Why use components and $ref? How do you mark a field nullable in 3.1 versus 3.0? When do you use oneOf versus allOf, and what does discriminator do?

chapters.title: Design-First vs Code-First, Clients and Contract Testing
points: Design-first: write the spec before code, review it with consumers, then generate stubs and mocks; Code-first: derive the spec from annotations or framework models (FastAPI, springdoc), so docs match the code by construction
Pick design-first for public or multi-team APIs where parallel work and the contract matter; pick code-first for fast internal services owned by a single team

Generate clients and server stubs with openapi-generator (openapi-generator-cli generate -i openapi.yaml -g typescript-axios -o ./client) or openapi-typescript for types only; regenerate in CI and never hand-edit the output

Contract testing: Schemathesis (schemathesis run openapi.yaml --url http://localhost:8000) fuzzes the live API against the spec; Dredd and Prism proxy/validate requests and responses against it; consumer-driven Pact checks what consumers actually use
Interview Point: Compare design-first and code-first and say when to choose each. How do you generate and version a client? What does contract testing catch that unit tests miss?

chapters.title: Keeping Docs in Sync and Common Mistakes
points: Lint the spec in CI with Spectral (spectral lint openapi.yaml) using a ruleset for naming, required descriptions and operationId rules; also validate it with redocly lint
Detect breaking changes by diffing against the main branch (oasdiff breaking old.yaml new.yaml); removed fields, new required params and narrowed enums should fail the build
Single source of truth: either the spec generates the code, or the code generates the spec and CI fails if the committed file is stale; a hand-edited spec next to hand-written code drifts

Common mistakes: missing error responses, undeclared required fields (properties are optional unless listed in required), duplicate operationIds, loose schemas with no additionalProperties decision, and examples that don't match the schema
Interview Point: How do you stop the spec drifting from the implementation? What counts as a breaking change? How would you wire OpenAPI checks into CI?

chapters.title: OpenAPI Cheat Sheet
points: Skeleton: openapi: 3.1.0, info {title, version}, servers, paths, components {schemas, parameters, responses, securitySchemes}, security, webhooks
Operation checklist: operationId, parameters (in + required), requestBody.content, responses by status code, security, tags
Schema keywords: type, properties, required, enum, items, format, allOf/oneOf/anyOf, discriminator, $ref; nullable is type: ['x','null'] in 3.1
Commands: spectral lint, redocly lint, openapi-generator-cli generate -g <lang>, schemathesis run, oasdiff breaking
Rule of thumb: spec is the contract; generate code from it or it from code, lint it and diff it for breaking changes on every PR; test the running API against it
Interview Point: Summarise the end-to-end contract workflow from authoring a spec to detecting a breaking change. Which tools sit at each stage?
